stories.headline: Colorado AG sues GEO Group over refusal to comply with tuberculosis investigation at Aurora ICE facility
stories.summary:
The Colorado Attorney General's Office filed a lawsuit Wednesday against GEO Group, the private company that operates the Aurora ICE Processing Center, alleging the firm failed to comply with a state public health order related to a tuberculosis investigation. The lawsuit came days after GEO missed an Aug. 17 deadline set by the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment, which confirmed an active tuberculosis case at the facility in June.

Since that confirmation, the Adams County Health Department and state health officials repeatedly requested information and facility access from GEO, but the company declined each time. Attorney General Phil Weiser said GEO is "endangering Coloradans' public health" by refusing to follow the state health department's order and violating Colorado law.

A GEO spokesperson maintained there are currently no active or suspected tuberculosis cases at the facility and said the company has provided information to state and county officials as authorized by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, adding that both DHS and the CDC are actively involved in disease control measures. State health officials said those assurances are "reassuring" but not a substitute for compliance with a legally issued health order.

The lawsuit demands GEO provide what officials described as "critical information" necessary to complete the investigation. Health officials emphasized that GEO has a responsibility not only to detainees inside the facility but also to employees and the surrounding community.

stories.headline: Waymo driverless robotaxis set to launch in Denver later this year
stories.summary:
Waymo is preparing to launch its driverless robotaxi service in Denver before the end of 2026, with autonomous vehicles already spotted training on city streets ahead of a public rollout. The company's product innovation manager, Chris Bonelli, demonstrated the technology during a media ride Tuesday, showcasing van-like vehicles equipped with sliding doors, large interior monitors, and passenger controls for temperature and seating.

Bonelli emphasized safety as a central feature, citing a 94% reduction in serious injury or fatal crashes in cities where Waymo already operates. During the demonstration ride, the vehicle encountered a blocked street caused by tree trimmers and connected with Waymo's remote support team to navigate around the obstacle.

No specific public launch date or Denver pricing has been announced. Waymo said its Denver fleet will include technology capable of clearing snow from sensors and adjusting driving behavior for snow, slush, and ice — addressing a key concern for Colorado residents considering the service.

Some Denver residents expressed curiosity tempered by caution, with several comparing the experience to a novelty similar to a roller coaster ride. Others indicated they would try the service if pricing is competitive with existing rideshare options.

stories.headline: Infleqtion opens 80,000-square-foot Colorado Quantum Innovation Center in Louisville as company reaches $3 billion valuation
stories.summary:
Infleqtion, one of the largest quantum computing companies in the United States, officially opened its new 80,000-square-foot headquarters in Louisville on Tuesday, consolidating its previously split offices in Louisville and Boulder into a single facility at 1315 W. Century Drive. The company branded the space the Colorado Quantum Innovation Center rather than a corporate headquarters, positioning it as a hub for the broader quantum industry.

CEO Matt Kinsella described Colorado as the epicenter of what he called the "quantum revolution," dubbing the region "Quantum Peak" in a comparison to Silicon Valley. The company, which went public on the New York Stock Exchange in February with a valuation of $1.8 billion, has since grown to a market capitalization of approximately $3 billion.

Infleqtion traces its roots to 2007, when CTO Dana Anderson founded ColdQuanta based on Nobel Prize-winning research conducted at the University of Colorado Boulder and the National Institute of Standards and Technology. The company, which rebranded to Infleqtion in 2023, works on quantum computers, atomic clocks, and quantum gravity gradiometry devices for both government and commercial clients.

State and regional leaders attended the opening ceremony. Jesse Olsen, CEO of the Boulder Economic Council, noted that Infleqtion "grew out of Colorado's quantum ecosystem, helped strengthen that ecosystem, and is now choosing to once again invest in its future here."

stories.headline: Colorado math scores reach record high for fourth consecutive year; Denver-area district results vary widely
stories.summary:
Colorado students posted record math scores on the 2026 Colorado Measures of Academic Success exam, with 37.3% of students meeting or exceeding expectations — up from 35.9% last year and the fourth straight record high, the Colorado Department of Education announced Wednesday. English scores remained essentially flat, dipping slightly from 44.8% to 44.7%.

Education Commissioner Susana Córdova acknowledged the gains while noting that fewer than half of students are meeting expectations in either subject, underscoring that reaching pre-pandemic levels does not equate to high performance. The results reflect a persistent achievement gap between math and English proficiency statewide.

Across the Denver metro area, results varied sharply by district. Littleton Public Schools led locally with 58.4% math proficiency, followed by Douglas County at 57.2% and Boulder Valley at 56.2%. Denver Public Schools recorded 35% math proficiency and Aurora Public Schools posted 20.5%, both below the state average.

The CMAS is administered annually to third- through eleventh-graders and serves as the only consistent statewide measure of student achievement across all schools. The release also included PSAT and SAT college readiness data.

stories.headline: Denver set to approach daily heat record Friday as city logs 50th day above 90 degrees in 2026
stories.summary:
Denver climbed back into the 90s Wednesday and is forecast to remain there through Friday, with Friday's afternoon high potentially approaching the daily record of 99 degrees set in 2023, according to Denver7 meteorologists. Wednesday marked Denver's 50th day of 90-plus-degree temperatures in 2026, already above the annual average of 46 such days.

Wednesday also brought isolated severe storms to the eastern plains and heavy downpours that triggered flash flood warnings for Pueblo and the nearby Aspen Acres Fire burn scar. Forecasters said they will continue monitoring the potential for dangerous flooding and debris flows in that area through the end of the week.

Thursday and Friday will see chances for stray showers and storms across the high country and along the Interstate 25 corridor. Storm chances are expected to increase over the weekend as temperatures begin to cool, with highs dropping to the upper 80s by early next week.

stories.headline: Bear breaks into Mount Crested Butte home, accidentally starts kitchen fire
stories.summary:
A bear entered a home in Mount Crested Butte early Wednesday and unintentionally started a fire in the kitchen, according to the Crested Butte Fire Protection District, which posted about the incident shortly after 3 a.m. Firefighters were able to contain the flames to the kitchen and no injuries were reported.

The incident comes amid what Colorado Parks and Wildlife officials describe as a near-doubling of bear encounters across the state compared to 2025. Separately, CPW is also investigating a bear that broke into a home near Fish Creek Falls Road in Steamboat Springs and struck a woman in the face when she tried to chase it out, and another bear attack was reported in Aspen on Wednesday.

Authorities are urging residents to lock doors and windows while away or sleeping, secure food and trash, and clean outdoor grills. Officials advise against approaching bears or attempting to remove them from a home, recommending instead that residents leave an exit route for the animal and call 911 immediately.

stories.headline: Federal judge says 'smoking-gun' email links Trump administration directly to retaliation against Colorado
stories.summary:
A federal judge has described a newly surfaced email as a "smoking gun" linking the Trump administration directly to alleged retaliation against Colorado, according to reporting published Wednesday. The development marks a significant escalation in an ongoing legal dispute between Colorado and the federal government.

Details of the specific retaliation alleged were not fully elaborated in available reporting, but the judge's characterization of the email as direct evidence of administrative intent represents a potentially pivotal moment in the case. Colorado has been among the states engaged in litigation with the Trump administration over several federal policy disputes.

The ruling or finding adds to a series of legal clashes between Colorado state officials and the federal government and could influence the trajectory of related cases pending in federal court.

stories.headline: Denver moves to shut down Five Points nightclub after security guard accused of sexual assault at gunpoint
stories.summary:
The City of Denver is moving to shut down a nightclub in the Five Points neighborhood after a security guard at the establishment was accused of sexually assaulting a patron at gunpoint, according to reports published Wednesday. The action represents a formal city effort to revoke the venue's operating license or permit in response to the alleged incident.

Details of the assault allegation and the identity of the nightclub were part of the public record in the city's enforcement action. Denver officials cited the severity of the alleged conduct as grounds for the closure proceeding.

The move reflects broader city efforts to hold entertainment venues accountable for the conduct of their security personnel. The case remains under investigation by Denver police.

stories.headline: Front Range law enforcement agencies to conduct coordinated crackdown on expired vehicle registrations starting Aug. 23
stories.summary:
The Colorado Springs Police Department announced Wednesday that it will lead a coordinated, week-long enforcement effort targeting expired and unregistered vehicles on Front Range roads beginning Aug. 23. Participating agencies include the Denver Police Department, Aurora Police Department, Colorado State Patrol, and departments from Monument, Palmer Lake, Fountain, and El Paso County.

Officials said the surge enforcement was prompted by residents' concerns about the rising number of vehicles with expired or missing registrations. Law enforcement said it will take a zero-tolerance approach to violations from Aug. 23 through Aug. 28.

The stated goal of the operation is to encourage compliance with vehicle registration requirements and remind owners of their legal responsibilities. Residents can renew registrations and access additional resources through the Colorado DMV website.

stories.headline: Rockies swept by Dodgers at Coors Field, extending franchise-record 19 consecutive series without a win against Los Angeles
stories.summary:
The Colorado Rockies were swept by the Los Angeles Dodgers at Coors Field this week, dropping all three games by scores of 11-5, 7-6, and 6-4 in 10 innings. The sweep extended Colorado's franchise-record stretch to 19 consecutive series without a series win against the Dodgers, surpassing the previous mark of 12 straight series against the Phillies from 2007 to 2021.

Shohei Ohtani dominated the first two games with four hits and two home runs Monday and another homer Tuesday, though his 22-game Coors Field hitting streak was snapped in the series finale. Mickey Moniak hit his 20th home run of the season in Game 3 to tie the score in the seventh, becoming the first Rockies outfielder with consecutive 20-plus home run seasons since Charlie Blackmon, but Los Angeles scored twice in the 10th inning to close out the sweep.

Los Angeles won the 2026 season series 10-3 against Colorado, and it marked the eighth time the Rockies were swept this year. Starting pitchers Tomoyuki Sugano, Ryan Feltner, and Kyle Freeland each took losses, with Freeland exiting Game 3 in the fourth inning with neck tightness after a strong stretch to open August.

Manager Warren Schaeffer said the team fights hard every night regardless of the opponent but acknowledged that coming close is not the end goal. The Colorado bullpen offered a relative bright spot, posting a 2.55 ERA over its last six games.

stories.headline: Rockies' Zac Veen and Cole Carrigg emerge as energetic centerpieces of Colorado's rebuild
stories.summary:
Outfielder Zac Veen and rookie utility player Cole Carrigg are drawing attention as a pair of high-energy, speed-driven young players at the center of the Rockies' long-term rebuilding effort. Veen, the No. 9 overall pick in 2020, is hitting .333 with improved plate discipline through his first six games of 2026 following a dominant Triple-A summer and his work addressing substance abuse issues.

Veen's instincts were on display last weekend in San Francisco, when he bolted home after a catcher failed to field a blocked pitch cleanly, scoring in a play that highlighted his aggressive, instinct-based style of play. Manager Warren Schaeffer credited Veen's off-field maturity as the most significant factor in his development.

Carrigg, who debuted June 9 after being selected in the second round of the 2023 draft, is slashing .284/.367/.474 with five home runs and 34 RBIs in 58 big-league games while providing defensive versatility in center field and shortstop. Both players rank in the top 15% of baseball in sprint speed.

"They are two players who play without fear and don't care what it looks like out there," Schaeffer said. Veteran outfielder Mickey Moniak called Carrigg's emergence a reflection of the kind of hungry, free-playing mentality the organization wants from its young core.

stories.headline: Avalanche face critical offseason decision as Artturi Lehkonen enters final contract year
stories.summary:
The Colorado Avalanche are facing a pivotal roster and financial decision heading into the 2026-27 season as forward Artturi Lehkonen enters the final year of his contract. Lehkonen has been a key contributor on Colorado's top lines and penalty kill since joining the team, making his contract status one of the more significant questions facing the organization this offseason.

The Avalanche must weigh the cost of a long-term extension against their existing salary cap commitments, with several other core players already under contract at significant figures. A failure to re-sign Lehkonen could create a gap on a team that has relied on his two-way play and postseason experience.

No extension talks have been publicly reported at this stage, and the situation will draw increasing attention as the regular season approaches. How the Avalanche handle Lehkonen's situation is expected to be a defining question of their front office's offseason management.

topStory.headline: Missouri Judge Allows Trump-Backed Congressional Map to Stand for November Elections
topStory.summary:
A Missouri state judge ruled Wednesday that new U.S. House district boundaries backed by President Donald Trump will remain in effect for the November 2026 general election, rejecting an effort to place the Republican-drawn map before voters in a statewide referendum. Cole County Circuit Judge Daniel Green ruled that Missouri's constitutional referendum provisions do not apply to congressional redistricting enacted by the state Legislature, siding with Republican officials who argued the General Assembly holds sole authority over such maps.

Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins had already blocked the referendum effort on primary day in August, refusing to certify a petition carrying thousands of signatures on the grounds that the state constitution does not permit a public vote on congressional redistricting. Judge Green upheld that refusal, ordering that the new map "remains in full force and effect for the 2026 general election." Opponents of the plan, led by Richard von Glahn of the group People Not Politicians, announced an appeal the same day, with von Glahn stating the case would ultimately be decided by the Missouri Supreme Court.

The new map was drawn after Trump urged Republican-led state legislatures to redraw congressional boundaries ahead of the midterm elections. Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe called a special legislative session for that purpose last year, resulting in a map designed specifically to weaken Democratic U.S. Rep. Emanuel Cleaver's hold on his Kansas City-based 5th Congressional District. The redraw breaks portions of Kansas City into neighboring Republican-held districts and extends the remainder of Cleaver's district eastward into heavily Republican rural territory, with approximately 59 percent of voters in the reshaped district being new to it.

Missouri's current U.S. House delegation stands at six Republicans and two Democrats. A successful Republican effort to flip Cleaver's seat would further expand the GOP's majority in the closely divided U.S. House. With an appeal now filed and the Missouri Supreme Court likely to have the final word, the legal fight over the map is expected to continue even as candidates campaign under the new boundaries.
